content: 1. A small group and plenary review typically focuses on a limited number of functions. A debrief After Action Review (AAR) is generally informal and centers on the specific operations of a single team. Its scope is narrow, allowing for targeted learning outcomes. 2. A working group AAR employs an interactive and structured methodology, combining group exercises, plenary discussions, and facilitation techniques. It integrates group work (6–12 participants per group) with plenary sessions. Each working group corresponds to a specific pillar of the response, such as surveillance or case management. Regular plenary sessions facilitate shared learning, consensus building, and validation of recommendations across technical working groups. These sessions also enhance understanding of interdependencies between disciplines and stakeholders. This format can accommodate a large and diverse group of participants, often exceeding 20 individuals. 3. A key informant interview AAR involves a more in-depth review of an event. It includes research into background materials, such as peer-reviewed literature, media reports, and grey literature. This is followed by semi-structured interviews and short focus group discussions, where key informants are encouraged to provide candid feedback on their experiences. Surveys may also be used to gather feedback, which can help triangulate common points of information from interviews and focus groups. Findings are analyzed and synthesized into a concise report with key recommendations, which is then shared with participants for validation. Confidentiality and non-attribution are critical components of this AAR format. 4. A mixed-method AAR combines elements of debrief, working group, and key informant interview formats. This approach is particularly useful for reviewing responses to emergencies where it may not be feasible to convene responders in a working group format. Key informant interviews are conducted prior to group work, and their results inform subsequent group discussions. The findings from both processes are synthesized into a final report for validation. 5. AAR formats are flexible and should be adapted to the culture and practices of the institution, organization, or agency conducting the review. Planners can use specific questions to determine the most appropriate format, such as whether it is practical to bring stakeholders together, the scope of the review, and the availability of resources. 6. Building an AAR team involves defining roles based on the chosen format. Key roles include the overall AAR lead, lead facilitator or interviewer, facilitators and interviewers, note takers, and a report writer. The AAR lead is responsible for planning and conducting the review, liaising with senior management, and compiling the final action plan. Facilitators guide discussions, ensure focus, and manage conflicts, while note takers document discussions. The report writer consolidates inputs into a final report. 7. Developing a budget early in the process is essential to secure necessary funding. Budget templates are available in AAR toolkits. 8. Preparing a checklist and draft agenda helps streamline the preparation phase. Checklists ensure readiness, while draft agendas provide structure for the review process. Examples of these are included in AAR toolkits. 9. A concept note summarizes key information agreed upon during the design phase. It is used to gain support and commitment from senior management and encourage partner participation. A template for the concept note is available in AAR toolkits. 10. Stakeholders and facilitators should be informed about the AAR process, format, objectives, and their roles. Email templates for this purpose are included in AAR toolkits. 11. The venue for the AAR should be chosen based on the format. For working group formats, the venue should accommodate plenary sessions, group discussions, and have sufficient wall space for posting results. 12. Preparing for an AAR involves several key actions, including collecting and reviewing relevant background information, refining trigger questions, and briefing facilitators and interviewers. Background materials may include emergency response plans, situational reports, and outbreak reports. Trigger questions should be open-ended and tailored to the context and objectives of the review. 13. Facilitators and interviewers should be impartial and fluent in the language of participants. They should have a sound understanding of the technical areas under review and be skilled in guiding discussions and summarizing key points. 14. A coordination meeting should be held several days before the AAR to familiarize the team with objectives, agenda, roles, and trigger questions. For key informant interview AARs, a preliminary meeting ensures consistency in interview conduct and information capture. 15. During the AAR, the opening session should provide participants with a common operational and contextual understanding of the event. The lead facilitator introduces the agenda, objectives, scope, methodology, and expected outputs. Generic PowerPoint presentations to support this stage are available in AAR toolkits.
